item.description:

Release Notes:
Version 1.2.1 Log Continuity Manager 1.2.1 focuses on Mass Interruption monitoring, delivery visibility, Search Head Cluster readiness and AppInspect compatibility. New Features \- Added Mass Interruption Policies for detecting widespread log interruptions across monitored hosts. \- Added Host Count and Percentage threshold types. \- Added Policy Scope support for: \- All monitored targets \- host\_index \- host\_index\_source \- host\_index\_sourcetype \- Added optional exact Source and Sourcetype filters for scoped Mass Interruption policies. \- Added Mass Interruption, Reminder and Recovery email notifications. \- Added configurable subject templates for Mass Interruption notifications. \- Added Suppress New Individual Interruption Emails option during active mass incidents. \- Added Current Mass Incidents visibility. \- Added Current Mass Notification Delivery status. \- Added Recent Mass Notification Delivery history with sent and failed delivery visibility. \- Added delivery history time filters. Mass Interruption Improvements \- Mass Interruption calculations use normalized unique hosts. \- Percentage thresholds are calculated against the scoped eligible host population. \- Maintenance-suppressed, redundancy-suppressed and disabled targets are excluded from evaluation. \- Scope information is shown in incident status and email content. \- Source and Sourcetype scoped policies are supported without affecting unrelated monitoring targets. \- Existing policies remain backward compatible and default to All monitored targets when scope fields are absent. Notification Reliability \- Improved Mass Interruption notification claim and scheduler handoff reliability. \- Added safer stale/orphan claim handling. \- Preserved duplicate-send protection and notification fencing. \- Improved runtime lock contention handling with bounded retry behavior. \- Improved handling of deleted and disabled Mass Interruption policies. \- Added clearer visibility for interruption, reminder and recovery delivery states. KV Store and SHC Improvements \- Runtime application state is persisted in KV Store. \- Improved Search Head Cluster compatibility for application state. \- Added safer runtime locking behavior. \- Preserved current-state and historical notification data across normal app upgrades. \- Improved Unicode handling for user-entered fields such as Owner and Description. AppInspect and Compatibility Improvements \- Resolved blocking AppInspect failures. \- Resolved Python-related Future Failure findings for custom commands, alert actions and REST handlers. \- Added explicit Python 3 interpreter requirements where required. \- Improved web.conf and custom configuration reload compatibility. \- Improved package/version metadata validation. Short Description:
A Splunk app for monitoring log continuity, detecting individual and mass interruptions, tracking recovery, and managing monitoring targets with KV Store-backed state.


Description:
Log Continuity Manager for Splunk helps teams detect, manage and investigate log ingestion interruptions across monitored hosts, indexes, sources and sourcetypes. The app supports target-based continuity monitoring, interruption detection, recovery tracking, maintenance and redundancy-aware handling, and operational dashboards for monitoring status and history. Version 1.2.1 adds Mass Interruption monitoring with Host Count and Percentage thresholds, scoped policies for host_index, host_index_source and host_index_sourcetype targets, interruption/reminder/recovery email notifications, notification delivery visibility, KV Store-backed runtime state, and improved Search Head Cluster readiness. The app is designed for Splunk Enterprise environments where continuous log visibility and rapid identification of ingestion gaps are operationally important.

item.title: Contrast Security ADR for Splunk - v1.2.4 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
\- Dashboards and the app's Search menu link now use the \`contrast\_search\` macro instead of the \`contrast\_adr\` event type. They follow the index set in the macro and no longer depend on the user's default search indexes. \- Fixed the Application filter on the Attacks by Applications dashboard. Selecting an individual application previously returned no results, because the filter compared application names against the application ID field. \- The Attacks Blocked chart on the Attacks by Applications dashboard now groups by application name instead of application ID. \- Fixed the Attack Dashboard drilldown from the Attacks by Applications chart, which returned no events for application names containing spaces. The attacked URL drilldowns now quote the clicked value too. \- Fixed the Command Injection, Cross-Site Scripting, HTTP Method Tampering and XML External Entity Injection correlation searches, which never matched ADR events. They now filter on the rule IDs ADR sends (\`cmd-injection\`, \`reflected-xss\`, \`method-tampering\` and \`xxe\`). \- The attack type correlation searches now also match ADR semantic sub-rules, for example \`sql-injection-semantic-tautologies\`. \- The Exploited Attack Event, WAF, EDR, DLP and incident correlation searches and their drilldowns now use the \`contrast\_search\` and \`contrast\_inc\_search\` macros instead of event types, so they no longer depend on the user's default search indexes. \- The \`contrast\_search\` and \`contrast\_inc\_search\` macro definitions are now wrapped in parentheses, so they combine safely with \`OR\` and other search terms. \- Removed \`state\_change\_requires\_restart\` from \`app.conf\` to meet the Splunk Cloud Platform vetting requirements. Enabling, disabling or upgrading the app no longer forces a Splunk restart. \- Removed the unused \`\[triggers]\` stanza from \`app.conf\`. The app does not ship \`passwords.conf\` or \`user\_configuration\` settings.


Description:
Contrast Security Application Detection & Response (ADR) for Splunk allows you to secure running applications like never before. Contrast Security ADR for Splunk provides timely actionable attack exploit events across the entire application portfolio. Contrast Security instrumented applications self-report the following about an attack – the attacker’s IP address, authenticated username, method of attack, which applications, servers, frequency, volume, level of compromise, and more. In addition, Contrast Security can block these attacks in real time while also providing specific guidance to engineering teams on where applications were attacked and how threats can be remediated. Finally, Contrast Security's Log Enhancement capability extends this visibility into the inner workings of application and user behavior. Log Enhancers enable users to log anything in an application.

item.title: Cyera TA - v4.1.45 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
**Audit collection now uses the Cyera Events API.** The audit input (`cyera:audit`) now collects from the Events API `Authentication` category. The sourcetype name is unchanged and no reconfiguration is required. Access to the Frontegg audit API will be deprecated in Cyera v41, so upgrade before v41 to keep audit data flowing. **Events API audit records for every events input.** After the upgrade, every input with **Collect Events** on automatically writes Events API authentication records to `cyera:audit`, whatever the legacy checkbox says. Collection starts from the input's existing events checkpoint, and earlier records are not backfilled. **Legacy Frontegg collection continues by default until v41.** On upgrade, an input that already collected Frontegg audit logs keeps collecting them alongside the Events API records. The new global setting **Legacy Frontegg audit collection** (Configuration > Add-on Settings) ships set to **Default**, which preserves existing behavior. New inputs don't collect Frontegg audit logs. The per-input checkbox **Collect Legacy Frontegg Audit Logs (deprecated — stops working in Cyera v41)** is unchecked for new inputs. Set the global setting to **Off** to stop Frontegg collection early. When Cyera v41 deprecates the Frontegg audit API, Frontegg collection stops working and the add-on reports it as an error. At that point, set the global setting to **Off**. Legacy collection will be removed in a later add-on release. **Updated Audit Trail dashboard and data model.** Both now use the Events API fields `type`, `outcome`, `ip`, `userAgent`, and `email`. The release adds three panels: **Failed Authentications**, **Authentication Outcomes Over Time**, and **Top Source IPs**. **Configuration Changes** is renamed **Provisioning Changes (SCIM)**. Newly included events are failed sign-ins and SSO sign-ins, MFA enrollment prompts and failed MFA verifications, password resets, signups, lockouts, IP-policy blocks, and SCIM user and group provisioning. The Login KPIs and the `Cyera_Login` event type count only Events API records. **CIM Authentication mapping.** For Events API records, `action` and `result` are `success` or `failure` (from `outcome`). The readable event label, such as "Login", "SSO Login", or "SCIM User Create", is in `vendor_action` and `signature`. `user` is the email when present, otherwise the user ID, and `src` is the IP address. Legacy Frontegg records keep their original `action` text, for example "User logged in", which is also copied to `vendor_action`. **Government (FedRAMP) support.** Audit collection and the Audit Trail dashboard are now available in the Government environment, which records successful sign-in, SSO sign-in, and sign-out events. item.description:

Release Notes:
Bare -k \ flag, mirroring ausearch -k \: filters events by the auditd watch key set via auditctl ... -k \. Unlike -i/-correlate (single-token boolean flags), -k's value is a separate SPL token with no \= in either part, so \_protocol\_v2\_option\_parser() now carries a small piece of state across sequential calls to merge the two tokens into key\=\. -k, -k\=\, --key, --key\=\, and the existing key\=\ are all equivalent and can be freely mixed with -i in any order (auditsearch -i -k rootcmd and auditsearch -k rootcmd -i behave identically). A bare -k with no following value now reports a clear error via the Job Inspector instead of silently doing nothing or crashing.


Short Description:
Bring practical ausearch-style interpretation and filtering to raw Linux auditd events directly inside Splunk. AuditSearch performs search-time processing without modifying indexed events or requiring source-side parsing, Python, ausearch, or additional software on monitored Linux systems.


Description:
AuditSearch is a Splunk custom search command that brings practical ausearch-style interpretation and filtering capabilities directly into the Splunk search pipeline for raw Linux auditd events. AuditSearch is designed around a simple principle: keep the original auditd event untouched and perform interpretation at search time. Instead of modifying audit logs before they reach Splunk, installing additional parsing software on monitored Linux systems, or transforming auditd events into another format at ingestion time, AuditSearch operates on the events already indexed in Splunk. With the auditsearch command, security analysts and engineers can interpret supported auditd fields and apply audit-specific filters directly from SPL. Supported functionality includes interpretation of fields such as arch, syscall, PROCTITLE, negative exit values as errno, and supported hexadecimal audit fields. Original field values are preserved using the corresponding _raw fields, allowing analysts to work with decoded values while retaining the original representation for verification and forensic analysis. AuditSearch supports both ausearch-style syntax and Splunk-style argument forms. Common options include: -i for auditd field interpretation -k or key= for filtering by auditd key type= for filtering by audit record type auid= for filtering by login UID For example: index=linux_audit sourcetype=auditd | auditsearch -i -k rootcmd type=EXECVE auid=1000 | table _time host auid comm exe PROCTITLE AuditSearch performs its processing at search time and does not require ausearch, Python, a custom scripted input, or an AuditSearch-specific Add-on on the source Linux systems. Existing auditd forwarding configurations can remain unchanged. The command is designed for Splunk environments where raw Linux auditd data is already being collected and analysts need practical interpretation and filtering capabilities without changing the source-side audit pipeline. Because AuditSearch performs search-time processing, users should filter events as much as possible before invoking the command. Narrowing the event set with indexed fields, host, time, event type, UID, or other available filters can reduce the processing required by the command. AuditSearch is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

Short Description:
Send Splunk the logs that sampling and filters keep out to fit the license, on that same license. Compact events take a fraction of the volume and expand back byte-identical at search time; classic dashboards keep their SPL, and one command covers the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API.


Description:
With the Log10x App, Splunk can index compact log events and still search, chart and alert on the original lines. The 10x Receiver stores each event as a template hash plus the values that change, so a stream of repeated patterns takes less of the license. On the OpenTelemetry demo the bytes sent to Splunk shrank by 63.7%, encoded events and template dictionary counted together, and every line expanded back byte-identical with the Receiver settings in the installation steps (measurement: https://www.log10x.com/blog/cutting-splunk-log-storage/). The same license then holds more: sources that were sampled, filtered or kept out of Splunk to stay under the limit can come back, or the license can be smaller. Classic dashboards keep their SPL: the browser sends each panel's search to the app, which rewrites it on the server. From the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API, a search is wrapped in the tenxsearch command. An alert created in the app's Compile Alert view is compiled once into a native saved search, so the scheduler runs no Python. NOT, OR, groups, phrases, field conditions, and values such as IP addresses and hostnames behave as they do on the original data. The 10x Receiver produces compact events, and it is free on up to 10 nodes (https://www.log10x.com/pricing). No sign-up is required to evaluate it: with no license token it runs the full product for 30 days on up to 10 nodes, air-gapped, and a free license removes the time limit (https://doc.log10x.com/manage/license/). The app itself is open source under the MIT license.

Monitor when every index, sourcetype and host last sent data and get alerted when logs stop arriving. Detection uses receive time, so clock or time zone issues don't cause false outages. Description:
Log Source Monitor tracks when every log source last sent data to Splunk and alerts you when data stops arriving. A log source is each unique combination of index, sourcetype and host, so you see exactly which firewall, server or application went silent and for how long. Detection is based on when data was received rather than on event timestamps, so sources with time zone or clock problems do not show up as false outages. You can set different delay and outage thresholds per index, sourcetype or host using wildcard rules. Alerts fire once when an outage starts and once when it recovers, instead of repeating every few minutes. The app also inventories every index with its size, retention and 24-hour activity, and shows forwarders that have disconnected or are connected but not sending data. It runs entirely on the search head, stores its data in the KV Store, and needs no Python, scripted inputs or custom indexes.

Description:
Darkmoon Pentest brings your Darkmoon AI penetration-testing results into Splunk and closes the loop back to Darkmoon. A producer — the bundled forwarder or a Darkmoon Pro webhook — sends safe JSON events to the HTTP Event Collector. The app parses them into CIM-aligned sourcetypes (darkmoon:campaign, darkmoon:finding, darkmoon:retest, darkmoon:pr) mapped to the Vulnerabilities data model, so findings sit alongside the rest of your security data. Evidence, secrets, credentials, tokens and request/response bodies are never ingested, with index-time redaction as a second line of defense. Six SOC dashboards give analysts an immediate picture: an Overview of KPIs and posture, Findings with full filtering, MITRE ATT&CK and Technology coverage, Campaigns, Remediation and Retest tracking, plus Setup and Help. Every panel drills down from posture to campaign to finding. For Darkmoon Pro users, the "Send to Darkmoon" alert action turns Splunk into an offensive-validation trigger: a correlation search can launch a retest or a new campaign, hard-secured with a target allowlist, a safe-harbor default, a token stored encrypted in storage/passwords, rate limiting, TLS verification and a dry-run default. item.title: HoneyLabs Intelligence - v1.2.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
1.2.0 is built for the triage queue rather than the demo. New feed input, fingerprints: TLS (JA4) and HTTP request (Akin) fingerprints the HoneyLabs sensors saw from 20 or more addresses in the shape of a scanning tool, with population counts and the port and path they favour. A scheduled search keeps it in the honeylabs\_fingerprints lookup, so a lookup on the JA4 field of your own TLS logs (Zeek ssl.log carries one) flags a scanning client on your perimeter with no API call, even when the address is clean. The Triage dashboard gains a fourth panel on it. Without a key the feed carries the 500 most widespread shapes of the last 7 days; with a free key stored on the setup page the input pulls the full list over 30 days. The honeylabs enrichment command returns honeylabs\_cves: the CVEs whose exploit paths the address probed in the last 7 days, so an alert can say what the address was after and a correlation search can join it against what you are exposed to. honeylabssearch mode\=similar takes an Akin token from your own web, WAF or proxy logs and returns the request shapes within a few headers of it, what those clients ask for, and the family it belongs to. Three alerts ship switched off, each with a 24 hour throttle per indicator: inbound from active exploiters, outbound to captured malware infrastructure, and a coordinated scanner client on the perimeter. Every row carries an evidence link. HTTP request fingerprints are Akin tokens (https://github.com/honeylabshq/akin). fp\_type\=akin works in mode\=fingerprint and mode\=population, and mode\=events takes an akin\= filter. fp\_type\=ja4h reports that the type was retired instead of failing the search.


Short Description:
Threat intelligence from live honeypot sensors, in SPL. Enrich any IP field with a verdict, ASN, ports and first and last seen, or query the dataset directly: raw probes, request payloads, CVE exploitation, JA4 fingerprints, top attackers. Plus two hourly threat feeds. Free API key gives 500 lookups a day; no key gives 10.


Description:
HoneyLabs runs open-source honeypot sensors on the public internet. Nothing reaches them by accident, so every connection they record is a scan, a probe, a brute-force attempt or an exploit. There are no false positives to filter out, because there is no legitimate traffic to confuse them with. This app puts that dataset inside Splunk. Two search commands. The first enriches addresses you already have. Point it at any field holding a public IPv4 address and it annotates every event: index=firewall | honeylabs field=src_ip | where honeylabs_events > 0 It writes back verdict, verdict_key, network_type, events, first_seen, last_seen, country, asn, asn_org, rdns, top_port, ports, exploit_hits and reference, each prefixed honeylabs_ so nothing collides with your own fields. Addresses are de-duplicated per search, so an index carrying the same scanner across ten thousand events costs one lookup. The second queries the honeypot dataset directly, with no local data required. Nine modes cover raw events, captured request payloads, top attackers, timelines, ASN profiles, TLS and HTTP fingerprints, IOC and CIDR lookups, CVE exploitation, and fingerprint population counts. Use it to answer questions your own logs cannot: who else is exercising this CVE, what payload is being sent, which other sources share this JA4 fingerprint. Two modular inputs, shipped disabled, index active exploiter addresses and captured malware staging URLs on an hourly schedule. Neither needs credentials. Two dashboards ship with the app: an overview of what the feeds currently carry, and an explorer for querying the dataset without writing SPL by hand. About the API key. The app installs and runs with no account and no setup, but anonymous use is capped at 10 lookups a day, which is enough to try the commands and not enough to work with. A free key raises that to 500 a day and takes about a minute to create at https://honeylabs.net/dashboard. Paste it into the app's setup page; it is stored through Splunk's storage/passwords, encrypted at rest, and never written to a .conf file. Paid plans go to 50,000 a day. On privacy: a lookup sends only the public IP addresses in your search. Not your index, host, source or sourcetype names, not your Splunk version, not the search string. Private, loopback, link-local, multicast and reserved addresses are filtered out locally before the request is built. The feed inputs are ordinary HTTPS downloads of a public file and disclose nothing at all. Running Enterprise Security? Load the indicator feeds through its own threat intelligence framework so they reach correlation searches and risk scoring rather than only being searchable, and keep these commands for on-demand investigation. Walkthrough: https://honeylabs.net/integrations/splunk-es

item.title: Supply Chain and AI Threat Intelligence Platform - v1.2.17 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:

SCIP v1.2.17 — MITRE ATLAS coverage expansion, severity re-rating, compliance citation corrections, and audit fixes

This release consolidates the work in v1.2.15, v1.2.16 and v1.2.17 since the last published release (v1.2.14). The AI/agentic detection library grows from 66 to 81 rules (72 MITRE ATLAS-mapped, 9 vendor-defined). No cryptographic surface was modified.

New detections (15)

Fifteen new AI and agentic threat detections were added, covering: an AI service API used as a covert command-and-control channel; AI supply-chain rug pulls, where an established component's newly published content turns malicious; artifact repositories used as dead-drop C2 channels; agent runtime capability discovery; and sub-technique coverage for dataset and capability acquisition, autonomous exploit and agent tool development, system prompt and instruction discovery, agent tool data collection, tool runtime response poisoning, and poisoned model, dataset and agent-tool publication.

Separately, two existing detections gain additional technique tags, for multimodal prompt-injection triggers and for misconfigured or publicly exposed AI services. These are more precise labels on rules that already shipped, not new detections.

Detection accuracy and severity

  • Every ATLAS rule and the SBOM Drift Monitor now set alert.severity as an integer. String values were being coerced by Splunk and read back as 0, so triggered-alert severity in Splunk and any alert action keyed on it were unusable. Emitted severity fields, lookups and dashboard behaviour are unchanged.
  • A severity rubric pass re-rated three rules added in the previous release and confirmed nine others.
  • Five MITRE ATLAS technique names and tactics were corrected to the catalog text, and coverage is now scoped against ATLAS 2026.09 with a recorded disposition for every technique added in that catalog release.
  • Three regression guards now run before every package build: one validates every technique stamp against the shipped lookup, including secondary stamps; one validates the severity mapping on every rule; and one verifies that shared facts agree across the README, the deployment guide and the shipped artifacts.

Compliance citation corrections

No assessment logic changed. Citations and control identifiers were corrected across seven of the nine frameworks SCIP assesses:

  • EU Cyber Resilience Act control IDs now use the regulation's own Annex and Article labels; two transposed points corrected; coverage added for two security-update provisions. Now 21 controls.
  • FDA 524B: transposed statutory citations corrected, the patch-cycle control re-cited, the cyber device definition restored to its three statutory prongs, and guidance-derived rows distinguished from statutory ones. Now 21 controls.
  • NIST CSF 2.0: 16 subcategory descriptions replaced with CSF 2.0 outcome text.
  • PCI DSS 4.0.1 and FedRAMP: requirement and control titles restored to official text.
  • HIPAA: four rows re-titled to the standard's own name; a control that was being assessed twice is now out of scope.
  • DORA: incident classification and ICT concentration risk re-cited.
  • A nightly cleanup now retires status records for controls that are no longer in scope, so renamed or descoped controls leave nothing frozen behind.
  • Compliance views and the CSV export now carry a Last Assessed column, flagging any status older than two days as stale.

Functional fixes

  • The POA&M population search collided its inline time bounds with its dispatch window and scanned nothing while reporting success.
  • Five scheduled searches stored a search string beginning with a literal search command, which silently excluded events whose raw text lacked that word.
  • Setup, Remediation Tracking and Telemetry Settings could write to the KV Store on page load, before any Save action. All three now write only on an explicit action.
  • Telemetry Settings rewrote the license collection on every page view; it now updates a single record on an explicit selection.
  • The license status check treated a record with a missing or non-numeric expiry as active.
  • Risk score pruning deleted rows with a missing or non-numeric timestamp; those rows are now retained.
  • Incomplete SBOM baseline rows no longer suppress the set-a-baseline prompts or count toward baselined-application totals.

Setup and onboarding

  • The Setup page now names every index SCIP requires, states that SCIP does not create them, gives both standalone and clustered paths, and warns when any is missing.
  • A new section explains that SBOM drift's component, version and count signals are inactive until a baseline is set.
  • The file monitor section states that both SBOM inputs ship disabled, that the monitored path must be repointed, and that SPDX files belong in their own directory.
  • NVD API key copy corrected in four places.
  • The license blocklist field no longer shows an internal placeholder on load, and the blocklist is emptied through an explicit Clear action.

Air-gapped and egress-restricted deployments

CISA KEV and EPSS threat intelligence can now be refreshed by file transfer, as NVD and OSV already could. Both feeds write normalized records to spool directories that new file-monitor inputs index. Previously both were script-only, so without outbound access they stayed frozen at install, silently degrading KEV-driven risk scoring. The IL Deployment Guide documents the record formats and procedure.

Roles and user experience

All three SCIP roles gain eleven read and UI capabilities that restore the Apps menu icons and the Setup credential-status read. The administrative role retains the capabilities its credential-save controls require.

Documentation

New ATLAS coverage manifest and a guide to authoring your own ATLAS detections on top of the shipped baseline. The deployment guide now lists every required index in both its standalone and clustered instructions, documents scheduled searches that ship disabled by design, and corrects the outbound-connection table, which described telemetry as opt-out. Telemetry is opt-in and off by default.

Upgrade notes

  • Role assignment. SCIP roles are additive. If a user was assigned a SCIP role as their only role, they have been without the top-right username and account menu since v1.1.11. Assign your organization's base Splunk role alongside the SCIP role.
  • Saved-search renames. EU CRA and FDA compliance saved searches were renamed to match their new control identifiers. Any local override or external reference to the old stanza names must be updated.
  • Alert severity. Triggered-alert severity now reports real values instead of 0. Alert actions keyed on severity will begin seeing 2 through 5.
  • HIPAA control count drops from 9 to 8 in-scope controls. The descoped control's saved search is disabled rather than deleted, preserving the audit trail.


Short Description:
A Splunk app that detects AI-threat patterns (MITRE ATLAS) and runs software composition analysis (SCA) on your SBOMs to identify known-vulnerable components (NVD, OSV) — surfacing the applications where both appear at once. Compliance evidence across nine frameworks and FedRAMP/RMF audit exports, with no separate platform to stand up.


Description:
SCIP is a Splunk app that detects adversarial AI/ML threats (MITRE ATLAS) and runs software composition analysis (SCA) on your SBOMs to identify known-vulnerable components (NVD, OSV) — then, through Compound Risk, surfaces the applications where an AI-threat detection and a known vulnerability appear at once, the exposure neither signal shows alone. It prioritizes with CISA KEV and EPSS and assesses compliance posture across nine frameworks — detection logic written as transparent SPL you can open and read, and no separate platform to stand up. item.title: Supporting App for Oracle SBC CDR - v1.0.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
* CRITICAL: disconnect\_cause was declared twice in the Stop record field list, at positions 17 and 134. Splunk took the first, so for three releases the field held Oracle's coarse outcome category and the Q.850 cause at position 134 had no field name at all and could not be searched. Position 17 is now cisco\_disconnect\_cause, which is Oracle's own name for it, and disconnect\_cause now holds the Q.850 cause. If you have saved searches or dashboards matching on disconnect\_cause values, they are matching the coarse category and need to move to cisco\_disconnect\_cause. * CRITICAL: calling\_mos, called\_mos, calling\_r\_factor and called\_r\_factor now hold the actual score. Oracle writes all four multiplied by 100 so that an integer attribute can carry a fraction - a MOS of 4.3 arrives on the wire as 430 - and the fields previously passed that through, so any threshold written against them was wrong by two orders of magnitude. The wire value is still available as calling\_mos\_raw and so on. A zero in these columns means the SBC has no QoS feature set enabled rather than a call scoring 0.0, so zero now reads as null. * The app now extracts a ciscoguid from accounting\_call\_id, so SBC records can be rolled up with CUCM, CUBE and CVP data where the deployment carries the identifier across. * Added worst\_mos and worst\_r\_factor, the score of the worse of the two directions. For some statistical analysis end-users will want to exclude the "not bad" side. These new fields will now let them do that more easily. * Oracle SBC CDR's two disconnect cause spaces are finally extracted as separate fields. Added q850\_cause\_description and cisco\_cause\_description, which describe the two cause spaces separately, from a new cause\_descriptions lookup. * the now-general "cause\_description" values now list the most specific reason available: the Q.850 cause where there is a meaningful one, and Oracle's coarse category where there is not. Prior to this release, cause\_description was simply giving the RADIUS accounting termination cause (still available as accounting\_termination\_cause\_description). * Added a ciscoguid\_family field, which reports whether a ciscoguid is an H.225-format guid or a time-based UUID. This was previously only available via a search macro that misreported any record carrying two guids. * The descriptions shown for SIP response codes, ie the sip\_status\_description field, have been rewritten from the IETF specifications that define each code - RFC 3261, plus the fifteen later RFCs that define the codes RFC 3261 does not cover. The codes themselves and their reason phrases (sip\_status\_code and sip\_status\_name) are unchanged. If you have saved searches, alerts or dashboards that match on the old description text rather than on sip\_status\_code, update them. * Added a health check that lists any saved search, dashboard or macro still using the old west/east media flow field names, with the name that replaces each. Run it as a user with admin\_all\_objects for a complete inventory. * Added a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md file to the app, itemizing the third-party components it bundles and the origin of the data in each of its reference lookups.

Release Notes:
* Fixed the party number extractions on records whose SIP display name contains a comma, as "Last, First" from a corporate directory does. The station id fields are quoted for that reason, but the extraction walked the line by commas without honouring the quoting, so such a record was read one field out of step: callingPartyNumber came out empty and calledPartyNumber held the CALLING party's number, while the real called number was lost. * These are index-time fields, so the correction applies to newly indexed data only. Events already in the index keep the shifted values.


Description:
This app provides the index-time configuration to ingest the CDR data from Oracle Session Border Controller (Oracle SBC) and also from Oracle Session Router. Specifically the CSV-formatted CDR format that you get if you enable local cdr storage on the oracle boxes. The app correctly separates the intermingled start, interim and end records of this dataset, into three distinct sourcetypes, and extract the fields from each correctly. Note that although you can use it purely to onboard the data, this app contains NO search-time config and will not by itself extract the search-time fields properly. This is because it is designed to always work in conjunction with Sideview's "Supporting App for Oracle SBC", which is to be installed on the Search Head and which handles the search-time field extractions among other things. Furthermore ,both of these apps together are also designed to work with Sideview's "Cisco CDR Reporting and Analytics" app. When all three pieces are used together, the solution gives users a more general Investigation and Reporting solution for Oracle SBC and Oracle Session Router. The use cases are actually nearly endless so please contact Sideview if you have questions or would just like to find out more. this app is a part of Sideview's overall Investigation and Reporting solution, and you can find more documentation on the Sideview website: https://sideviewapps.com/documentation/oracle-sbc-cdr
